5. Lhe Language and the Metres

In Kalidasa we find the normal state of the Prakrits in the
later drama, Cauraseni for the prose speeches, and MaharAstri for
the verses.’ The police offices and the fishe: in the Cakuntala
use Magadhi, but the king’s brothet-in-law, who is in charge of
the police and is a faint echo of the Caka1a, speaks, as we have
the drama, neither Caka1i nor Magadhi nor Daksinatya but simply
Cauraseni. By this time, of course, we may assume that Prakrit
for the drama had been stereotyped by the authority of Vara-
ruci’s Prakiit grammat, and that it differed considerably from
the spoken dialect ; there would be clear proof if the Apabhranca
verses of the Vekramorvagi could safely be ascribed to Kalidasa.
The Maharastri unquestionably owes its vogue to the outburst of
lyric in that dialect, which has left its traces in the anthology of
Hala and later texts, and which about the period of Kalidasa
invaded the epic.?
Kalidasa’s Sanskrit is classical ; here and there deviations from
the norm are found, but in most instances the expressions are
capable of defence on some rule or other, while in others we may
remember the fact of the epic tradition which is strong in Bhasa.
The metres of Kalidasa show in the Mdlavikagnimitra a
restricted variety; the Arya (35) and the Cloka (1 7) are the only
meties often occurring. In the Vikramorvagi the Arya (29) and
the Cloka (30) are almost in equal favou1, while the Vasanta-
tilaka (12) and the Cardilavikridita (11) make a distinct advance
in importance. In the Cakuntala the Arya (38) and Cloka (36)
preserve their relative positions, while the Vasantatilaka (30) and
Cardiilavikridita (22) advance in frequency of use, a striking
proof of Kalidasa’s growing power of using elaborate metrical
forms. The Upajati types increase to 16. The other metres
used in the drama are none of frequent occurrence ; common to
all the dramas are Aparavaktia,? Aupacchandasika,* and Vaitiliya,
Drutavilambita, Puspitagra, Prthvi, Mandakranta, Malini, Van-
gasthd, Cardilavikiidita, Cikharini, and Harini ; the Miélavikag-

4. Harsa’s Art and Style

. Comparison with Kalidasa is doubtless the cause why Harsa
has tended to receive less praise than is due to his dramas. The
originality of his Natikds is not perhaps great, but he has
effectively devised the plot in both; the action moves smoothly
and in either play there is ingenuity. The scene of the magi-
cian’s activity in the Ratnadvali is depicted with humour and
vivacity, the parrot’s escape and its chatter are sketched with
piquancy, and the exchange of costumes in the Ratndvalt is
natural and effective. The double comedy in the Priyadargika
is a happy thought, the intrigue in Act IV is neatly conducted,
so as to show us Vasavadatta in the light of an affectionate niece,
and the scene with the bee is attractive. It is true that the
plays are full of reminiscences of the Mélavikdgnimitra, such as
the escape in the Ratnuaévali of the monkey, and the monkey that
there frightens the little princess while Samkrtyayani is Kaugiki
revived. But in this artificial comedy elegance is sought, not
